title: The Wheatstone Bridge: A Galvanometer That Lies Still at Balance
topic: Wheatstone bridge — four resistors in a diamond with a galvanometer between the two midpoints; the two midpoints reach the same voltage when R1 over R3 equals R2 over Rx, and the meter falls dead still

beats.narration: Four resistors in a diamond, one tiny meter in the middle — how does this circuit measure resistance you cannot easily see?

elements.content: A diamond of resistors — when does the meter fall silent?

beats.narration: A battery drives two parallel arms. The top arm carries R one and R three; the bottom arm carries R two and R x. Between the two midpoints sits a galvanometer.

elements.content: Battery on the left, two parallel arms forming a diamond, four resistor zigzags, galvanometer circle between midpoints A and B

beats.narration: Each arm is just a voltage divider. The bridge is balanced — V A equals V B — exactly when R one times R x equals R two times R three.
Scrub R x. The galvanometer needle swings as the two midpoints disagree, then falls dead still the moment the ratio matches.

elements.content: Diamond bridge with R_x sweeping; galvanometer needle deflects left then right; live R_x readout; settles at balance with the needle vertical and a green dot.

beats.narration: At balance, the unknown comes straight from a ratio of three known resistors. That is why bridges measure strain, temperature, and tiny resistances better than any direct meter.

elements.content: compare, don't measure — that's how a bridge wins
